questions.stem: The central claim of the passage is that:
options: Information has become too expensive for ordinary people to obtain.
Entertainment is the main purpose of the modern information industry.
People today simply lack the willpower their ancestors had.
In an age of infinite information, human attention has become the truly scarce resource, and an industry now competes ruthlessly to capture it.
questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.passage: There is a peculiar economics governing the modern world, and its scarce resource is neither money nor land but attention. When information was hard to come by, the person who possessed it held the advantage; today, when information is effectively infinite and free, the advantage passes to whoever can capture the fixed and stubbornly limited hours of human notice. This inversion has consequences we are only beginning to understand. An industry has grown up whose entire business is not to inform us, nor to entertain us for its own sake, but to hold our gaze long enough to sell it on to someone else. The most sophisticated minds of a generation, it has been remarked, now spend their days engineering the small compulsions that keep a thumb scrolling. We are inclined to blame ourselves for the hours that vanish this way, to treat our distraction as a private failure of willpower. But this is to misread the contest badly. It is not a fair fight between an individual's self-control and a passing temptation; it is a fight between one tired person and thousands of talented engineers equipped with the most detailed map of human impulse ever assembled. To call the outcome a failure of willpower is rather like calling a flooded village a failure of swimming.

questions.stem: The main argument of the passage is that:
options: The capacity to be bored — to leave the mind unoccupied — has hidden value for creativity that the constant filling of every idle moment destroys.
Screens are the only reliable cure for boredom.
Boredom is always unpleasant and should be eliminated wherever possible.
Creative people are simply those who are never bored.
questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.passage: We have been taught to regard boredom as a void to be filled at the first opportunity, an itch that the nearest screen exists to scratch. Yet there is reason to think we are, in banishing boredom so efficiently, quietly impoverishing ourselves. The restless, unoccupied mind is not merely idling; left alone, it begins to wander, to make unexpected connections, to worry at half-formed problems that a busier mind would never have the leisure to notice. Many who have thought carefully about creative work report that their best ideas arrived not at the desk but in its absence — on a walk, in the bath, in the drowsy minutes before sleep — precisely when the mind was permitted to roam without a task. What such moments have in common is a certain emptiness, a gap in the day that the wandering mind rushes in to fill with its own strange productions. When every such gap is instantly plugged with a feed of novelty, we may be spared the mild discomfort of having nothing to do, but we forfeit the more valuable thing that discomfort was quietly making possible. Boredom, on this view, is not the enemy of a rich inner life but one of its unlikeliest tutors — and a civilisation that has abolished it may find it has thrown out something it did not know it possessed.

The greatest obstacle to knowledge, on this view, is not ignorance, which at least knows itself, but the (68)________ conviction that we have understood. It is frequently the most honest and the most (71)________ thing a thinker can say, for it alone leaves the door open through which new understanding might one day (72)________.
